item.title: Deriving an SBOM from closed firmware such as Citrix NetScaler
item.description:
When I wrote the first post about PHP2Shell on NetScaler, I had no idea it was going to be a series. But it has been an interesting deep dive, and every part answered a question by taking the firmware apart. Which PHP version does NetScaler run? Does it have ASLR? Did Citrix really fix it?

That worked, but it doesn’t scale. The next vulnerability will start with the same one: do we run this, and which version?

The official advice for PHP2Shell assumed you know that already. The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) keeps a php2shell repository on GitHub, and its first recommended action is to identify your PHP applications and their versions, starting with internet facing systems. It also points out that PHP is embedded in appliances and management interfaces. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says the same, and adds that you should consider taking a system offline if you can’t mitigate it quickly.

In my eyes, knowing what you have is one of the most important things in IT security. It’s also not the most exciting part. Companies like to invest in a SOC, and in tooling such as a SIEM, EDR, threat intelligence feeds and vulnerability scanners. But all of that builds on knowing what you run. It’s the foundation, even if it isn’t sexy.

For a closed appliance, that is the hard part. NetScaler customers couldn’t even tell which PHP version they had until someone looked inside, and the same goes for most firewalls, load balancers, VPN gateways and storage appliances. The industry answer to “know what you run” is an SBOM, a software bill of materials. So I tried: can you derive a usable SBOM from closed firmware yourself?

The experiment is generic. NetScaler is the test case because I already know its firmware from parts 1 to 3, so I can check the result against what I found by hand.

Disclaimer: this is my own static analysis of the firmware (build 14.1-73.46), not confirmed by Citrix. An SBOM only contains metadata (names, versions, hashes), no Citrix code. And a component or a CVE match in an SBOM means that a version is present, not that the appliance is exploitable. More on that below.

item.title: Did Citrix really fix PHP2Shell on NetScaler? Taking the patched firmware apart
item.description:
This is part 3 of my PHP2Shell on NetScaler series. In part 1 I showed that NetScaler 14.1-73.46 ships PHP 8.1.34 and is vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In part 2 I looked at how hard it would be to exploit.

Today Citrix updated its security bulletin CTX697263 with fixed builds:

  • NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.49 and later
  • NetScaler ADC and Gateway 13.1-64.32 and later releases of 13.1
  • NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.49 FIPS and later
  • NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.286 and later

The release notes for 14.1-73.49 say that it replaces 14.1-73.46 and addresses the vulnerabilities in CTX697263. That’s all: release notes don’t list security fixes, so there is no word about PHP or what was changed. So 73.46 is exactly the right build to compare with, and the binaries are the only place to see what Citrix did.

PHP 8.1 is end of life. The PHP project did publish the fix for 8.1, as a backport branch in their repository, but there is no new 8.1 build or release: no PHP 8.1.35. Anyone who still ships 8.1 has to take that source change and build PHP themselves. In part 1 I wondered if Citrix would backport the fixes to 8.1 or move to a newer, supported PHP version. Now we can check.

Jan Tytgat and I took build 14.1-73.49 apart and compared it with 14.1-73.46. We wanted to answer four questions, with evidence and not just the vendor’s word for it:

  1. Did Citrix backport the fixes to PHP 8.1?
  2. Is it the upstream fix, or did they write their own?
  3. What exactly changed in the code?
  4. Are the issues really fixed?

Disclaimer: this is our own static analysis of the firmware, not confirmed by Citrix. We analysed one build, 14.1-73.49, and did not run an exploit against it.

item.title: PHP2Shell on NetScaler: to ASLR or not to ASLR?
item.description:
Yesterday anyone in IT will have followed the news about the two PHP bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, better known as PHP2Shell. I wrote a post on what they mean for Citrix NetScaler on the day the PHP fixes came out, before Citrix had released a statement.

Since then more information has come out. One thing I read is that triggering the bugs is the easy part. Turning them into code execution requires memory addresses, and those are normally hidden by ASLR (address space layout randomization). Most of the proof of concept exploits on GitHub don’t work at all. The ones that do either brute force the addresses or need a separate memory leak.

VulnCheck says the same, more on that below.

That made me look at what else NetScaler is built on. PHP 8.1 is not the only end of life component: NetScaler runs on FreeBSD 11.4, stripped down and customised by Citrix, and that has been end of life since 2021. Every FreeBSD version that is still supported has ASLR switched on by default. So I looked at two things: does ASLR really matter for these bugs, and does NetScaler have it?

Disclaimer: this is based on the PHP advisories and fix, public analysis and my own static analysis of the firmware (build 14.1-73.46). It is not confirmed by Citrix. I did not build an exploit and I won’t publish one.

Update 27 October 2026: Citrix has released fixed builds for PHP2Shell. The fix is in the PHP code, the platform didn’t change: the patched build still runs FreeBSD 11.4 without ASLR. See part 3.

item.title: Does PHP2Shell reach NetScaler? Taking the firmware apart to find out
item.description:
On 21 October 2026 PHP released fixes for two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both pre-auth remote code execution and both CVSS 4.0 9.2. Public reporting calls the pair “PHP2Shell”. The worst case target in the advisories is Apache with mod_php.

NetScaler ships PHP as well. So the first questions from customers are easy to guess: which PHP version does NetScaler run, are we affected, where on the appliance does PHP actually run, and can it be reached from the internet?

This post is my answer for one firmware build, 14.1-73.46. The short version: yes, it is vulnerable, and I can show that in the disassembly, not just from a version number. But the vulnerable PHP only runs behind the management interface. The internet facing Gateway doesn’t reach it.

Disclaimer: until there is an official statement from Citrix, this is what I could determine from the public documentation and my own static analysis of the firmware. It is not confirmed by the vendor. Treat it as informed analysis, act on it carefully, and check it against the Citrix advisory once there is one.

Update 21 October 2026: a few hours after this post went live, Citrix published mitigation guidance. It confirms what I found: only the management interfaces are affected. See What Citrix says.

Update 22 October 2026: Citrix has published a security bulletin, CTX697263. It lists NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway as impacted and refers to the mitigation guidance above. There is no fixed build yet.

Update 22 October 2026: in a follow-up I looked at how exploitable this is on NetScaler, and whether NetScaler has ASLR. See PHP2Shell on NetScaler: to ASLR or not to ASLR?.

Update 27 October 2026: Citrix has released fixed builds (14.1-73.49, 13.1-64.32 and FIPS builds, see CTX697263). Citrix backported the fix to PHP 8.1, it did not move to a newer PHP version. Jan Tytgat and I took the patched firmware apart to check what Citrix changed, see part 3.

item.title: Analysing binaries with Binwalk
item.description:
I came across an interesting tool today called Binwalk.
Binwalk is a firmware analysis tool that scans a given binary file for embedded files and executable code.

 

Binwalk requires a Linux machine, I used the Backtrack VM I used from my article about WEP keys.

Note there is no binary distribution of Binwalk so you will need to compile it but this is a breeze.
